title: Having a Sweet Tooth Linked to Safer Choices
paragraphs: Some people enjoy the very occasional dessert. Others can't walk past a cake shop without looking through the window!
But could having a sweet tooth be connected to how you make decisions?

Researchers from Russia's National Research University Higher School of Economics thought so. They wanted to understand more about why people who respond strongly to rewards are more likely to make impulsive decisions. And they thought that people who prefer very sweet tastes would also be people who respond strongly to rewards.

Participants tasted sugar water at five different sweetness levels, and rated how pleasant each one was. Those who preferred the sweetest option were called "sweet-likers," while those who preferred less sweet options were "sweet-dislikers."
The researchers then looked at how these people made decisions about money.

First, they tested how willing participants were to take risks. Participants chose between a guaranteed amount of money and a chance to win more. But instead of showing a preference for the risky option, sweet-likers actually chose the guaranteed money more often.
Next, they looked at how willing people were to wait for rewards. Participants chose between a smaller amount of money sooner and a larger amount later.

When the smaller reward was available right away, sweet-likers were more likely to take it — which might be expected from a more impulsive person. However, when both options involved some waiting, sweet-likers were more likely to wait longer for the larger amount.
The researchers think these results may be connected, and noted that a future reward may feel less certain than one that's available immediately.
So sweet-likers may choose an immediate reward partly because it feels safer, rather than simply because they're impulsive and don't want to wait.

So, the study doesn't show that preferring sweet tastes — or responding strongly to rewards — really makes someone impulsive. Instead, these people may be more careful about taking risks, and this could affect the rewards they choose.
